patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed generalized seizure with preceding episodes of an unusual smell and a churning sensation in the stomach over the past several months
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kapoor is a 42-year-old left-handed elementary school teacher who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at his workplace. According to a colleague who witnessed the event, the patient was seated at his desk during a planning period when he suddenly stopped writing, appeared to stare vacantly at the wall, and then began making repetitive chewing movements. His left hand was noted to pick at his clothing in a purposeless manner. The colleague attempted to get his attention by calling his name and tapping his shoulder, but the patient was unresponsive. After approximately 20 seconds of this behavior, the patient's body stiffened and he fell from his chair onto the floor, developing rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly two minutes. He was placed on his side by another staff member who was CPR trained. A small amount of blood-tinged saliva was noted at the mouth. He was incontinent of urine during the episode. Emergency medical services arrived within eight minutes. On their arrival, the convulsive activity had stopped and the patient was in a post-ictal state, confused, drowsy, and unable to follow commands. He was transported to the hospital and gradually became more alert over the next 45 minutes.

Upon questioning in the emergency department, the patient recalls that immediately before the event he perceived an intense, unpleasant smell that he describes as similar to burning rubber or chemicals. This olfactory sensation was accompanied by a strong churning or fluttering feeling in his upper abdomen that seemed to rise toward his chest. He estimates these sensations lasted approximately 10 to 15 seconds before he lost awareness. He reports that he has been experiencing these identical episodes of the unusual smell and abdominal churning approximately two to three times per month for the past eight months. Each episode typically lasts 20 to 40 seconds. During most of these episodes he has been able to continue what he was doing, though he feels momentarily confused afterward. On two occasions his fiance observed his staring blankly for about half a minute and not responding when he spoke to her, after which he appeared dazed for a minute or two. He did not seek medical attention for these episodes because he attributed them to stress related to wedding planning and believed they might be panic attacks. He denies any history of prior convulsions. There has been no recent head trauma, illness, fever, sleep deprivation, or significant change in his medications. He denies alcohol or substance use around the time of the event.

results.title: Long-term epilepsy surgery outcomes in patients with DNETs
results.summary: Gross total resection of DNETs resulted in Engel class I (seizure-free) outcomes in 85% of patients at long-term follow-up. Incomplete resection was the main predictor of seizure recurrence.

results.title: Surgical treatment of epilepsy associated with dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors
results.source: Bilginer et al., Childs Nerv Syst 2009;25:1231-1237
results.summary: Complete lesionectomy with resection of surrounding epileptogenic cortex yielded seizure freedom in 80-90% of cases. Histopathological confirmation is essential for prognosis.

results.title: DNETs in adults: surgical outcomes and histopathological features
results.source: Lee et al., J Clin Neurosci 2018;56:74-79
results.summary: Adult patients with DNETs have excellent surgical outcomes comparable to pediatric cohorts. Duration of epilepsy prior to surgery did not significantly affect seizure-free rates, though earlier intervention is generally recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of right mesial temporal lobe origin secondary to dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET)

differential.key_features: Indistinguishable clinically from DNET; histology distinguishes.
MRI distinguishes a discrete lesion from sclerosis.
Can coexist with low-grade tumor (type IIIb FCD).
Aura with stereotyped automatisms is not syncope.
Migraine aura does not progress to a tonic-clonic seizure.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (routine first; pursue ambulatory or video-EEG if non-diagnostic) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize olfactory aura with epigastric / nausea sensation as a classic mesial-temporal seizure pattern.
Obtain MRI with contrast and dedicated epilepsy protocol.
Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy center / neurosurgery for resection planning.
Initiate first-line focal-epilepsy AED (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, lacosamide).
Counsel on driving restrictions and seizure-safety precautions.
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue an ENT workup for the olfactory hallucinations.
Do not perform LP without indication.
Do not start carbamazepine without verifying baseline sodium and HLA-B*1502 status if Asian ancestry suggests risk.
key_reasoning_points: Episodic olfactory + epigastric aura with witnessed GTC is highly localizing to mesial-temporal structures.
DNET / ganglioglioma are the most common surgical pathologies in adult-onset focal temporal epilepsy with a discrete lesion.
Surgical resection is potentially curative; AED therapy is bridging.
